title: Scale Shift
description: Scale shift cinematography changes a body's size against the same room so the figure is suddenly giant or tiny: Alice physics as an optical event. Furniture, shadows, and contact have to match the new ratio.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: A person stands in a kitchen and the table is a landscape. Or a hand is a building.
The geography did not cut. The scale did.
Use it when relative size is the plot of the shot. The same name is sometimes used for unequal story-time strands, as in Dunkirk's land, sea, and air clocks.
That is editorial scale, not optical size. Do not mix the two tools in one prompt.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Lock the room plate. Resize the figure with oversized furniture, miniatures, split-scale composites, or a cut that reprints the body at a new height in the same architecture.
Shadows and contact must match the new size: a giant throws a larger shadow from the same key. Forced perspective can help as a static alignment of two real sizes.
Prompt a scale shift of the subject: the body suddenly giant or tiny against the same room.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it for the beat when a person becomes a toy in their own hallway, or a monster in a dollhouse. Do not use it as a simple close-up that only magnifies a detail without changing the body-to-room ratio.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Forced Perspective aligns two real sizes on one focal plane so they look like one scale. Scale shift is the change of that relationship.
Magnification goes closer than a close-up, a world inside a centimeter. It does not make the whole body tiny in the room.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Honey, I Shrunk the Kids and Ant-Man stage bodies against furniture and grass at the wrong size. Dunkirk and Inception appear in the catalog as temporal-scale cousins: unequal clocks, not Alice rooms.
Use the first pair for optical size. Keep the second pair for editorial time.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Scale shift of [Subject], the body suddenly giant or tiny against the same room, Alice physics. Name the room, the new size, and matching shadows.
Ban a mere close-up and ban stretching the architecture.

Design an intercut rescue story: a mountain team’s six-hour ascent, a driver’s thirty-minute approach and a climber’s final two-minute wait. Build a timeline showing exactly where they converge. Generate separate location strands and edit them toward one shared radio call, not as falsely equal real-time durations.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousins are a Close-Up and a zoom. The tell is a big face with a normal room, or a lens punch with no furniture scale change.
The fix is the same architecture, a new body-to-room ratio, and contact that fits.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is scale shift in film?
A scale shift makes a body giant or tiny against the same room. Relative size changes as an optical event. A separate editorial meaning uses unequal story-time strands.
Scale shift vs forced perspective
Forced perspective is a static alignment of two real sizes so they read as one scale. Scale shift is the change: the body becomes the wrong size in a room we already know.
When should I use scale shift?
Use it when size is the joke or the threat inside a known space. Skip it when you only need a closer lens, and do not confuse it with intercutting unequal clocks.
How do I prompt scale shift for AI image or video?
Write Scale shift of [Subject], the body suddenly giant or tiny against the same room. Keep the architecture, match the shadows, and name the new size.
